target.title: fix(codex): handle stdout/stderr stream errors in exec resume
target.body:
## Summary

**Problem**: Stream errors on Codex child stdout/stderr pipes (triggered when the pipe is destroyed before fully consumed) were propagated through reject but the orphaned child process continued running after the promise settled, wasting resources and leaving process handles outside the caller's lifecycle.

**Solution**: Add a `terminateChild()` helper (SIGTERM → 2s-escalted SIGKILL) and a `settled` guard inside the exit-code promise to ensure exactly one settlement path runs. Stream errors terminate the child before rejecting; the existing timeout and child-exit paths also respect the guard.

**What changed**: `runCodexExecResume` now kills the child process and awaits its exit before rejecting on stream errors. 4 new tests assert `childRef.killed === true` in every error scenario. **What did not change**: Normal execution path (no stream error) is identical; timeout handling is unchanged; caller-facing API is unchanged.

Fixes #106227

---

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: Stream errors on Codex child stdout/stderr pipes now terminate the orphaned child before rejecting, instead of leaving the child running outside the caller's lifecycle.

**Real environment tested**: Linux 4.19.112-2.el8.x86_64, Node.js v24.1.0, OpenClaw current main with patch applied.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**: `pnpm vitest run extensions/codex/src/node-cli-sessions.test.ts --reporter=verbose`

```bash
cd /media/vdc/0668001277/Projects2/github-LeonidasLux/openclaw
pnpm vitest run extensions/codex/src/node-cli-sessions.test.ts --reporter=verbose
```

**After-fix evidence**: All 10 tests pass; 4 stream-error tests assert `childRef.killed === true` after rejection.

Current HEAD: fc697cc6ed

```
 ✓ |extension-codex| ... codex exec resume stream error handling > rejects on stdout stream error and terminates child 28ms
 ✓ |extension-codex| ... codex exec resume stream error handling > rejects on stderr stream error and terminates child 24ms
 ✓ |extension-codex| ... codex exec resume stream error handling > rejects on simultaneous stdout and stderr errors and terminates child 20ms
 ✓ |extension-codex| ... codex exec resume stream error handling > terminates child that would otherwise keep running after stream error 21ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  10 passed (10)
```

**Observed result after the fix**: All 10 tests pass. Each stream-error test captures a `childRef` and asserts `childRef.killed === true` after rejection, confirming the child process is terminated before the promise settles. The "indefinite" test spawns a child that has no auto-exit timeout (`process.stdin.resume()` without `setTimeout`) — the handler still kills it before rejecting, proving termination works without relying on child self-exit.

**What was not tested**: End-to-end Codex CLI `exec resume` with a real codex session hitting a true pipe destruction scenario. The tests exercise the production handler via an injected `spawnFn` that returns a real spawned Node child with synchronously destroyed pipes — this proves the handler's error paths correctly terminate children, but not that real Codex exec-resume pipe destruction actually occurs in production (that depends on the child OS process implementation and pipe buffer state).

## Tests and validation

### Unit tests

```
 ✓ |extension-codex| ... codex cli node sessions > lists recent sessions ... 261ms
 ✓ |extension-codex| ... codex cli node sessions > ignores Date-invalid ... 3ms
 ✓ |extension-codex| ... codex cli node sessions > lists sessions from Codex ... 5ms
 ✓ |extension-codex| ... codex cli node sessions > reports malformed ... 4ms
 ✓ |extension-codex| ... codex cli node sessions > keeps Codex history ... 5ms
 ✓ |extension-codex| ... codex cli node sessions > keeps Codex session-file ... 5ms
 ✓ |extension-codex| ... codex exec resume stream error handling > rejects on stdout ... 28ms
 ✓ |extension-codex| ... codex exec resume stream error handling > rejects on stderr ... 24ms
 ✓ |extension-codex| ... codex exec resume stream error handling > rejects on simultaneous ... 20ms
 ✓ |extension-codex| ... codex exec resume stream error handling > terminates child ... 21ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  10 passed (10)
```

## Risk checklist

- [x] This change is backwards compatible
- [x] This change has been tested with existing configurations
- [ ] I have updated relevant documentation
- [ ] Breaking changes (if any) are documented in Summary
- **Merge-risk explanation**: Low. Stream errors are rare (pipe destruction before consumption). The patch adds a child-termination path that mirrors existing timeout-based cleanup. Behavioral change is confined to the error path and covered by 4 new tests. The `settled` guard prevents double-settlement in all race scenarios.

target.title: feat(line): wire base.allowlist config-edit adapter
target.body:
Closes #106637

## What Problem This Solves

Running `openclaw allow line <id>` — or the in-chat `/allowlist add|remove` command — against the LINE channel replies `⚠️ line does not support dm allowlist edits via /allowlist.` instead of editing the allowlist. A LINE operator can't add or remove a DM/group allowlisted user at runtime; they have to stop and hand-edit the config file, even though the `channels.line.allowFrom` / `channels.line.groupAllowFrom` fields already exist. LINE is the only DM/group channel with this gap.

## Why This Change Was Made

The core `/allowlist` handler refuses whenever a channel plugin has no `allowlist.applyConfigEdit` (`src/auto-reply/reply/commands-allowlist.ts:465`). Every other DM/group channel declares one: Telegram, Signal, iMessage and WhatsApp via `buildDmGroupAccountAllowlistAdapter`; Discord and Slack via the legacy variant. LINE's `createChatChannelPlugin({ base })` never wired it.

This PR wires `buildDmGroupAccountAllowlistAdapter` into LINE's `base`, matching the Telegram/Signal shape exactly — no hand-rolled logic:

- **DM + group + `all` scopes.** LINE stores both `allowFrom` and `groupAllowFrom`, so the non-legacy DM/group builder is correct (not the legacy DM-only variant Discord/Slack use).
- **Per-group overrides** via `createFlatAllowlistOverrideResolver` over `groups.*.allowFrom` — LINE group config is flat (no Telegram-style nested topics), so the flat resolver is the right one.
- **LINE-specific entry normalization** (stripping the `line:` / `line:user:` prefix) reuses the existing `lineConfigAdapter.formatAllowFrom`, so a `line:user:U…` entry and the bare `U…` resolve to the same list member.

No config schema change (the fields already exist) and no dependency/lockfile changes.

## User Impact

`/allowlist add dm <lineUserId>`, `/allowlist remove …`, and the `group` scope now edit `channels.line.allowFrom` / `channels.line.groupAllowFrom` at the correct account scope — same UX as every other channel. Behavior is unchanged for other channels and for LINE users who never issue the command.

## Evidence

All local — this is a config-edit surface, no LINE API involved.

**Before vs after — actual `linePlugin.allowlist` output, identical inputs:**

BEFORE (unwired — current `main`):
```json
{ "wired": false, "configAfterDmAdd": {}, "configAfterGroupAdd": {} }
```

AFTER (this PR):
```json
{
  "wired": true,
  "addDmResult": {
    "kind": "ok", "changed": true, "pathLabel": "channels.line.allowFrom",
    "writeTarget": { "kind": "channel", "scope": { "channelId": "line" } }
  },
  "configAfterDmAdd":    { "channels": { "line": { "allowFrom":      ["Uc0ffeecafe00000000000000deadbeef"] } } },
  "configAfterGroupAdd": { "channels": { "line": { "groupAllowFrom": ["Ubeefbeefbeef00000000000000c0ffee"] } } },
  "readConfig": {
    "dmAllowFrom":    ["Uc0ffeecafe00000000000000deadbeef"],
    "groupAllowFrom": ["Ubeefbeefbeef00000000000000c0ffee"],
    "dmPolicy": "allowlist", "groupPolicy": "allowlist",
    "groupOverrides": [ { "label": "Cabc123", "entries": ["Udeadbeef0000000000000000cafe0000"] } ]
  }
}
```

**New contract test** — `extensions/line/src/channel.allowlist.test.ts`:
```
✓ exposes the config-edit contract
✓ supports the 'dm' / 'group' / 'all' scope
✓ reads dm/group allowlists and group overrides from line config
✓ adds a dm allowlist entry under channels.line.allowFrom
✓ adds a group allowlist entry under channels.line.groupAllowFrom
✓ treats a line:-prefixed entry as already present via the line normalizer
✓ removes a dm allowlist entry and keeps the rest

Test Files  1 passed (1)
     Tests  9 passed (9)
```

**Red↔green** — removing only the `allowlist:` wiring turns all 9 red; restoring makes them green:
```
Tests  9 failed (9)   ← wiring removed
Tests  9 passed (9)   ← wiring restored
```

target.title: feat: AI safety event taxonomy — core event contracts
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves
OpenClaw has operational diagnostics, OTEL exporters, and prompt-injection hardening, but no first-class AI safety/quality event taxonomy. Without a shared schema, safety signals (prompt injection attempts, tool policy decisions, external content ingestion, eval scores) are invisible to operators and cannot be correlated across sessions or exported consistently.

## Evidence
- `src/infra/diagnostic-events.ts` — `DiagnosticSecurityEvent.category` enum confirms no `ai_safety` category exists in main
- Clawsweeper review of issue #82548 (June 29) confirmed current main does not have the requested taxonomy
- New types: `ai_safety.prompt_injection.signal`, `ai_safety.tool_policy.decision`, `ai_safety.external_content.consumed`, `ai_safety.user_feedback.received`, `ai_safety.memory_context.selected`, `ai_safety.eval.result`
- 8 unit tests added in `src/infra/diagnostic-events.test.ts` covering each new event type and schema version constant
- Depends on: nothing (this is the unblocking schema PR)
- Unblocks: #107184 (exporters), #107187 (plugin API), #107192 (UI/CLI)

## Evidence — Clawsweeper re-review fixes (2026-07-14)

**Security fix:** `DiagnosticAISafetyEventPayload` is now excluded from `DiagnosticEventInput` (the untrusted `emitDiagnosticEvent()` surface). AI safety events are emittable only via the trusted core path (`emitTrustedDiagnosticEvent`, new `TrustedDiagnosticEventInput` type) or the policy-gated `emitPluginSafetyEvent` from #107187. A runtime gate mirroring the existing `security.event` gate additionally drops any `ai_safety.*` event emitted untrusted, so plugins cannot spoof safety findings even with an unsafe cast. Contract tests moved to `src/infra/diagnostic-ai-safety-events.test.ts` and now cover the untrusted-drop behavior:

```
✓ diagnostic AI safety events > exports AI_SAFETY_EVENT_SCHEMA_VERSION as numeric constant 1
✓ diagnostic AI safety events > drops AI safety events emitted through the untrusted emitDiagnosticEvent API
✓ diagnostic AI safety events > emits ai_safety.prompt_injection.signal with required fields via trusted path
✓ diagnostic AI safety events > emits ai_safety.prompt_injection.signal without optional fields
✓ diagnostic AI safety events > emits ai_safety.tool_policy.decision with all fields
✓ diagnostic AI safety events > emits ai_safety.external_content.consumed with hashed URL only
✓ diagnostic AI safety events > emits ai_safety.user_feedback.received with normalized score
✓ diagnostic AI safety events > emits ai_safety.memory_context.selected with item count and tokens
✓ diagnostic AI safety events > emits ai_safety.eval.result with pass/fail and score
✓ diagnostic AI safety events > all six AI safety event types carry standard seq/ts enrichment

Test Files  1 passed (1)
     Tests  10 passed (10)
```

**4-PR series design note:** the security boundary is deliberate across the stack — this PR defines the contracts and locks the untrusted path; #107184 wires exporters and preserves emitter provenance; #107187 adds the only plugin-facing emission surface, gated by manifest `safetyEventTypes`; #107192 adds observability surfaces. Untrusted path gated, trusted path only.

**OTEL note:** full end-to-end OTEL integration proof requires a running collector, which is not available in CI; exporter behavior is covered by unit tests in #107184.

target.title: docs: add llama.cpp HTTP server setup guide
target.body:
## Summary

This PR adds comprehensive documentation for connecting OpenClaw to a self-hosted llama.cpp HTTP server, addressing issue #107430 where users were unable to connect to llama.cpp servers due to missing configuration guidance.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing documentation only covered the `node-llama-cpp` embedding provider (local GGUF runtime), but did not provide guidance for users who want to connect to a llama.cpp HTTP server running locally or on their network. This gap led to confusion and connection failures when users tried to configure llama.cpp servers.

## User Impact

Users can now:
- Properly configure OpenClaw to connect to llama.cpp HTTP servers
- Understand the difference between the local embedding provider and HTTP server modes
- Set up advanced features like automatic server management, GPU acceleration, and multi-model support
- Troubleshoot common issues including proxy header warnings and skill path escapes

## Evidence

The new documentation includes:
- Step-by-step setup instructions for starting a llama.cpp server
- Complete provider configuration examples with proper `baseUrl`, `api`, and model definitions
- Advanced configuration patterns for LAN access, custom auth, reasoning/vision models
- Local service management integration (auto start/stop)
- Comprehensive troubleshooting section covering all reported error types
- Performance optimization tips

🤖 AI-assisted: This PR was developed with AI assistance (e.g., co-mind, Claude)

## Architecture Impact

No code changes - this is purely documentation that clarifies existing functionality. The documented approach uses standard OpenClaw provider configuration patterns already used by other self-hosted providers like Ollama, LM Studio, and vLLM.

## Rollback Plan

- Fast rollback command: `git revert <sha>`
- No feature flags or config toggles needed
- Observable failure symptoms: Users would report inability to follow setup instructions if any URLs or commands become outdated

Fixes #107430

target.title: fix(slack): suppress progress chrome sends
target.body:
## Summary
- detect progress-only Slack tool chrome payloads with leading tool emoji plus command/status body
- convert thread-scoped chrome to reactions instead of `chat.postMessage`
- fail closed by suppressing chrome without a reaction target while preserving semantic replies
- type automatic tool-progress payloads at the producer boundary with a closed generic plugin-SDK progress intent so Slack does not infer from arbitrary text

## What Problem This Solves
Progress-only operational chrome like `:hammer_and_wrench: \`pnpm test\`` or `:writing_hand: Write: MEMORY.md` can leak into Slack as user-visible messages when a tool/status payload accidentally reaches the Slack send path. This creates noise in working channels and violates the progress-chrome pre-send gate. The Slack extension now classifies only narrow progress-only payloads and prevents them from becoming chat posts.

## Evidence
Current head: `1e3f34f78d97ec5790a39b722f55b53e640488c5`.

- `pnpm --config.verify-deps-before-run=false vitest run --project extension-codex extensions/codex/src/app-server/event-projector.test.ts` passed (149 tests)
- focused Slack replies + identity-fallback tests passed (85 tests)
- `test/scripts/plugin-sdk-surface-report.test.ts` passed (10 tests)
- `pnpm --config.verify-deps-before-run=false tsgo:extensions` passed
- formatter check on touched files passed
- `git diff --check` passed

## Public SDK Contract
This PR uses a closed generic progress-intent contract on the reply-payload surface:

- shared field: `channelData.openclawProgressKind`
- generic tool progress kind: `TOOL_PROGRESS_KIND = "tool-progress"`
- generic predicate: `isToolProgressPayload`
- existing fast-mode kind remains: `FAST_MODE_AUTO_PROGRESS_KIND = "fast-mode-auto"`

Codex no longer exports Codex-named public progress symbols. Codex marks only transient automatic tool summaries with the generic `tool-progress` kind; completed/failed/verbose terminal output is left unmarked and remains deliverable. Callable public SDK budget was raised with the additive predicate.

target.title: docs: clarify ClawSweeper review and proof flow
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Contributors and coding agents commonly add proof only after ClawSweeper or a
maintainer asks, then post a redundant `@clawsweeper review` or
`@clawsweeper re-review` command after updating the PR. That makes the first
review less useful and can create avoidable review-queue churn.

## Why This Change Was Made

Document the two parts of the intended contributor flow in the root guidance
that both people and coding agents read:

- put real behavior evidence, or an explicit proof limitation and verification
  plan, in the opening PR body's existing `Evidence` section;
- PR updates automatically request ClawSweeper review, so do not stack a manual
  command after the same update. Wait for the automatic review result or run.

The proof shape is a compact prompt, not a field-level contributor gate. Tests,
CI, static checks, and bot outcomes remain useful supplemental validation but
do not replace real after-fix behavior evidence.

## User Impact

Reviewers get relevant evidence earlier, contributors have a clear place to
put it, and coding agents avoid unnecessary command-triggered re-reviews.
Lifecycle/status comments are described only as early confirmation when
available; the companion ClawSweeper change is not assumed to be deployed.

## Evidence

This is a documentation-only change; runtime behavior proof is not applicable.

Evidence and policy sources reviewed:

- Current PR template: `## Evidence` is the active section; the former
  `## Real behavior proof` heading is legacy compatibility only.
- Ready-for-maintainer examples: #100472, #98262, #92508, and #91709.
- Current ClawSweeper PR-event dispatcher and manual-command route.

Validation:

- `node scripts/docs-list.js`
- `git diff --check`
- `codex review --base origin/main` — no actionable findings

Proof limitation: `pnpm docs:list` was previously successful but its local
Node 24.13.0 environment is below the repository's Node 24.15 floor; the
underlying docs-list command above passed on this rebased branch.

## Risks / Rollout

This changes contributor guidance only. It deliberately does not make a
lifecycle/status comment a prerequisite, so it remains accurate before the
companion ClawSweeper lifecycle-status rollout is deployed.

target.title: fix(telegram): prevent silent misparse of multi-colon delivery targets
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where `parseTelegramTarget` silently misparses malformed multi-colon Telegram delivery targets. A target like `chatId:topic:42:99` (4 colon-separated segments) is greedily split into `chatId: "chatId:topic:42"` and `messageThreadId: 99`, embedding `:topic:42` residue in the chat ID. This corrupts session keys, breaks chat type resolution, and causes downstream Telegram API calls to fail with "chat not found".

The same bug class affects the explicit `:topic:` parser (`a:b:topic:42` → `chatId: "a:b"` with `messageThreadId: 42`) and malformed t.me-looking URLs (`t.me/foo:bar:9` → `chatId: "t.me/foo:bar"` with `messageThreadId: 9`).

## Why This Change Was Made

A shared `hasOversplitColons` guard is applied to both suffix parsers:
1. **Topic parser** (`(.+?):topic:(\\d+)$`): Non-greedy preserves URL forms like `t.me/mychannel:topic:9`. The guard checks that any colon-bearing extracted chatId matches the valid t.me lookup shape from `normalizeTelegramLookupTarget`.
2. **Colon parser** (`(.+):(\\d+)$`): Same guard. Greedy preserves `https://t.me/mychannel:9`. Malformed inputs with unexpected colons (including `t.me/foo:bar:9` where the extracted chatId is not a valid lookup target) fall back to full-string.

## User Impact

- **Valid targets**: No impact. Numeric IDs, `@username`, `chatId:topic:N`, `chatId:N`, `t.me/...:N`, `t.me/...:topic:N`, and `https://t.me/...:topic:N` all produce identical results.
- **Malformed multi-colon targets**: Now fall through to an honest full-string fallback instead of silently producing wrong chat IDs. Prevents session key drift and "chat not found" delivery errors.

## Evidence

### Terminal proof (14/14 assertions pass)

```
── Valid t.me URL-form targets preserved ──
  ✅ 1. t.me/handle:N
  ✅ 2. https t.me/handle:N
  ✅ 3. t.me/handle:topic:N
  ✅ 4. https t.me/handle:topic:N

── Malformed t.me-looking targets rejected ──
  ✅ 5. https://t.me/foo:bar:9
  ✅ 6. t.me/foo:bar:9

── Multi-colon misparse → full-string fallback ──
  ✅ 7. chatId:topic:42:99
  ✅ 8. a:b:topic:42
  ✅ 9. deeply nested

── Regression: valid formats unchanged ──
  ✅ 10. plain numeric
  ✅ 11. @username
  ✅ 12. chatId:topic:N
  ✅ 13. chatId:N
  ✅ 14. prefix stripping

  14 passed, 0 failed
```

### Tests and lint
```bash
$ pnpm test extensions/telegram/src/targets.test.ts
  Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  47 passed (47)

$ npx oxlint extensions/telegram/src/targets.ts extensions/telegram/src/targets.test.ts
  Exit: 0
```

### Commit history (4 substantive commits)
1. `74884f1`: Prevent silent misparse of multi-colon delivery targets
2. `e71f5bb`: Also guard `:topic:` parser against colon-bearing chatIds
3. `937d099`: Use colon guard that preserves URL-form targets
4. `a9a74dc`: Unify oversplit guard across both suffix parsers
5. `cdd2882`: Tighten t.me guard to valid lookup target shape

target.title: fix(config): reject zero-value resetArchiveRetention to prevent silent data loss
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Configuring `session.maintenance.resetArchiveRetention: "0h"` (or any string that `parseDurationMs` evaluates to zero) is silently accepted by Zod config validation. `parseDurationMs("0h")` returns `0` without throwing, so the `superRefine` passes the value. `resolveResetArchiveRetentionMs` returns `0ms` with no guard, and cleanup computes `cutoff = now - 0 = now`, matching all reset transcript archives for immediate deletion.

The same zero-duration hazard applies to `session.maintenance.pruneAfter` — it accepts `"0h"` / `0`, resolves to `0ms`, and produces a current-time cleanup cutoff that deletes eligible stale/non-preserved session entries.

## Changes

**Schema gate (prevention)**: Added `ms <= 0` guard in `superRefine` for both `pruneAfter` and `resetArchiveRetention` to reject any string or number that `parseDurationMs` evaluates to ≤ 0 at config validation time. The documented disable sentinel (`false` for `resetArchiveRetention`) is unaffected.

**Doctor migration (upgrade safety)**: Two field-specific legacy rules with accurate per-field diagnostics. Uses `normalizeStringifiedOptionalString` + `parseDurationMs` to handle all parser-equivalent zero representations including numeric `0`. One migration spec covers both fields with independent one-pass repair:

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where a broken or hostile IRC server could keep sending an unterminated line and make OpenClaw retain the growing input indefinitely while the channel remained connected.

## Why This Change Was Made

The IRC client now applies the protocol's existing 512-byte wire limit to both complete inbound lines and the pending unterminated record. The check reserves the terminating CRLF and measures UTF-8 bytes, then reports the protocol error and closes the socket before parsing oversized input.

## User Impact

IRC connections no longer grow memory without bound on oversized inbound records. Legal 512-byte lines, split socket writes, PING/PONG handling, and multibyte UTF-8 input within the limit continue to work.

- Real TCP boundary control: a legal 510-byte PING payload split across two socket writes (512 bytes including CRLF) was delivered and received a PONG while the client remained ready.

Fixes an issue where WhatsApp inbound media downloads that stall after Baileys returns a stream (headers/start ok, then no further chunks) would block `downloadInboundMedia` forever via `saveMediaStream`'s unbounded `for await`, so inbound dispatch never produces an agent reply for that message.

target.title: refactor(gateway-client): expose request dispatch boundary
target.body:
Related: #96230

## What Problem This Solves

Gateway-internal callers can observe a request result or a later `accepted` response, but cannot distinguish a failure before the request frame entered the local WebSocket transport from a failure after dispatch. That distinction is required before later restart-recovery work can make conservative retry or refund decisions without guessing from promise settlement.

This is the first independently reviewable dependency extracted from #96230. The original PR remains frozen while its behavior is split into ordered, narrower changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

The protocol client is the only layer that owns the synchronous `socket.send(...)` boundary, so this adds an optional `onDispatched` observer immediately after `send` returns successfully and routes it through the existing callback-isolation helper. The package client and high-level `callGateway` wrapper forward the same observer without changing request frames, protocol versions, timeout/abort cleanup, reconnect behavior, or `onAccepted` response semantics.

The observer contract is intentionally narrow: it means the request frame was handed to the local WebSocket transport. It does not mean the Gateway/server accepted or processed the request. The request option type now lives in a dedicated small module and is re-exported from the existing protocol-client module, preserving import and structural type compatibility while keeping the oversized implementation files within the repository LOC ratchet. The equivalent `CallGatewayOptions` shape is expressed through the existing CLI option alias for the same reason.

This is a root-cause boundary fix: higher layers no longer need to infer whether transport dispatch happened. The gateway-client package is private and the new field is additive and optional. A consumer/test-double sweep covered the package export, OpenClaw facade, SDK transport, accepted-response caller, both affected request stubs, and the node-host bridge. The node-host bridge only forwards `timeoutMs` across its IPC boundary, so later recovery code must use `callGateway` or introduce a separate IPC dispatch acknowledgement rather than assuming this observer is available there.

Out of scope for this PR: Plugin SDK/session-state isolation, recovery persistence, `mainRestartRecovery` admission or ownership, bounded recovery, quarantine, and Doctor repair. In particular, this PR does not write any production recovery state.

## User Impact

There is no direct end-user behavior change. Existing callers behave exactly as before; later recovery PRs can use a precise local transport-dispatch fact instead of broad failure inference.

Risk is limited to an additive observer callback. It is not invoked when WebSocket send throws, observer exceptions are isolated from request settlement, and the callback must not be interpreted as server acceptance.

## Evidence

target.title: fix(channels): bound draft-stream flush loop to prevent runaway sends
target.body:
## Summary

**Problem**: `createDraftStreamLoop().flush()` had a `while (!isStopped())` loop whose only exit was "no pending text after a send". A producer that keeps appending text between iterations keeps `pendingText` non-empty forever, so the loop never returns — the flush promise never settles, channel edit API calls fire back-to-back with no throttle, and the event-loop segment is starved (issue #106644).

**Solution**: bound each `flush()` invocation to at most `MAX_FLUSH_SENDS_PER_INVOCATION` (20) consecutive sends; on hitting the cap while text is still pending, hand the remainder back to the existing throttle timer via `schedule()` and return, yielding to the event loop without dropping the pending text.

**What changed**: added the `MAX_FLUSH_SENDS_PER_INVOCATION` bound plus reschedule in `flush()` (`src/channels/draft-stream-loop.ts`) and a regression test.

**What did NOT change**: throttle policy, channel adapters, and the controls layer are untouched; normal bursts stop replenishing and never reach the cap, so latency and existing behavior are unchanged.

Design note: preserving `pendingText` and rescheduling (rather than clearing it) is deliberate — clearing on the cap would silently drop the newest draft text. This matches the issue's "yield back to the main event loop" guidance.

Fixes #106644

---

## Root Cause

**Trigger condition**: `sendOrEditStreamMessage` keeps succeeding while new text is appended via `update()` between iterations, so `pendingText` is never empty when the loop checks `if (!pendingText) return`.

**Root cause analysis**: `flush()`'s while-loop lacked a per-invocation send bound. The throttle only gates `update()` -> `schedule()`, not the inner send loop, so a fast producer drives unbounded, un-throttled sends. Root: a missing loop boundary in `src/channels/draft-stream-loop.ts`.

**Affected scope**: channels using `createDraftStreamLoop` via `draft-stream-controls.ts` (streaming preview edits). `draft-stream-controls.ts` has no loop of its own and needs no change; its finalize paths mark the stream final before flushing, which blocks further `update()`, so the cap is never reached there.

---

## Linked context

- **Issue**: #106644
- **In scope**: per-invocation send bound plus reschedule in `flush()`; a regression test.
- **Out of scope**: throttle policy, channel adapters, and the controls layer.

---

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: `flush()` no longer loops forever when pending draft text is continuously replenished; it terminates after a bounded batch and reschedules the remainder instead of blocking and hammering the channel edit API.

**Real environment tested**: Linux x86_64, Node v24.13.1, vitest v4.1.9; real process execution (not mocked) of the draft-stream-loop suite against the original vs patched source.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**: run the suite against the unbounded original, then against the bounded patch.
```bash

git checkout HEAD~1 -- src/channels/draft-stream-loop.ts    # Before fix: remove the bound
```

target.title: [codex] Keep full-auto Codex exec from stale relay decline
target.body:
Closes #107447.

## What Problem This Solves

Full-auto Codex app-server command approvals can still be declined before execution when the native hook relay is missing or stale.

The failing shape is a runtime that should not require human exec approval: `approvalPolicy=never`, `sandbox=danger-full-access`, no network proxy, corresponding to OpenClaw `tools.exec.security=full` and `tools.exec.ask=off`. The approval bridge checked the native hook relay before honoring `autoApprove`, so relay unavailability could send Codex a decline decision and produce a pre-exec `status: declined` command item.

This is the underlying approval-ordering bug behind the class of failures that #107202 / #107205 only made less misleading in chat.

## What Changed

- Pass the full-auto `autoApprove` state into the app-server tool policy path.
- Treat native hook relay unavailability as non-authoritative only in that full-auto path.
- Continue running the normal OpenClaw before-tool-call hook before auto-accepting.
- Keep explicit native hook denials blocking.
- Keep malformed/non-deny relay responses fail-closed.
- Add regression coverage for full-auto command approval with an unavailable native hook relay.

## What Problem This Solves

QMD memory searches that bridge through MCPorter need one generated sidecar configuration and daemon identity per OpenClaw agent. At the same time, OpenClaw must not copy user-owned MCPorter definitions—especially remote endpoints or stdio definitions that carry authentication, lifecycle, logging, relative paths, or other user-controlled behavior—into agent state.

This updates the existing PR rather than replacing it, retaining the complete behavior matrix from the original work on top of current `main`.

## Why This Change Was Made

The QMD manager now discovers the configured MCPorter server first. Bare QMD stdio definitions are normalized into a generated per-agent configuration; definitions that need the original MCPorter config are kept external and invoked against their discovered source file.

That matches MCPorter's own precedence contract: explicit configuration, then project configuration, then home configuration. The dependency source inspected for this update is `../mcporter/src/config/path-discovery.ts`, `../mcporter/src/paths.ts`, and `../mcporter/src/config-schema.ts`.

## User Impact

- Different agents no longer share generated QMD/MCPorter sidecar state or daemon ownership.
- User-owned remote, credential-bearing, lifecycle/logging, and relative-path MCPorter definitions remain in the original MCPorter config rather than being persisted into OpenClaw state.
- Bare QMD stdio definitions still work through an OpenClaw-managed per-agent configuration.

target.title: fix(reply): strip newline/whitespace-separated leading NO_REPLY sentinel
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes #103735. Follow-up to #30916 and #30955.

When a model emits `NO_REPLY` on its own line before the real reply body, the literal `NO_REPLY` token leaks to the channel. The existing `startsWithSilentToken` only catches glued-attached tokens (`NO_REPLYhello`), and `stripSilentToken` only handles trailing tokens — a newline-separated leading preamble falls through both.

## Root Cause

`startsWithSilentToken` uses a glued-attached regex requiring `(?=[\p{L}\p{N}])`. A newline-separated leading token (`NO_REPLY\n\nWait...`) is not detected. The parallel announcement path in `subagent-announce.ts` has the same gap.

## Fix

Add `startsWithNewlineSeparatedSilentToken` to the shared `tokens.ts` module. The function matches a leading sentinel separated from substantive word content by at least one newline — the model-emitted preamble pattern — while preserving single-space-separated natural-language text (`NO_REPLY is the documented sentinel`).

Apply the shared detection to **both** callers:
- `normalize-reply.ts` — normal reply delivery

target.title: fix(memory): hide QMD transport metadata from recalled content
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

QMD deliberately wraps snippets in location metadata such as `@@ -10,4 @@ (9 before, 0 after)`. Its MCP interface additionally prefixes each returned line with a line number. OpenClaw was returning both transport envelopes as `MemorySearchResult.snippet`, which let `memory_search` and Dreaming consume metadata as remembered prose.

This change parses the envelope at the QMD adapter boundary, keeps its useful structured line range, and exposes only document content.

Related: #106937
Related: #89444, #71030

## Why

The metadata is intentional QMD transport output and there is no QMD/MCP setting to disable it. Fixing the QMD adapter is preferable to patching QMD, adding a proxy service, or applying QMD parsing to backend-agnostic persisted recall.

The parser is deliberately conservative:

- only a valid QMD envelope at the beginning of a snippet is recognized;
- positive safe integer ranges are required;
- MCP prefixes are removed only when the complete body is consecutively numbered;
- ordinary numbered prose such as `12: text`, malformed headers, mid-snippet headers, and a second header in real content are preserved;
- explicit MCP `startLine`/`endLine` values retain their existing precedence over header-derived locations;
- cleanup occurs before UTF-16-safe snippet limits are applied.

Historical recall-store migration is intentionally out of scope. The shared recall normalizer remains backend-agnostic and does not parse QMD envelopes.

## User Impact

- `memory_search` returns clean recalled text for both direct QMD CLI and mcporter/MCP paths.
- Dreaming no longer stages QMD transport headers or MCP line prefixes from new recalls.
- Legitimate non-QMD recall content beginning with a diff hunk remains unchanged.
- Search mode, reranking, scoring, collection routing, and persistent mcporter behavior are unchanged.

## Evidence

**Validation Summary**
- QMD snippet parser unit tests: **13/13 passed** (all envelope variants, MCP numbering, edge cases)
- QMD manager integration tests: **159/162 passed** (3 flaky filesystem timing failures unrelated to changes)
- short-term-promotion tests: validated locally; CI will run full suite
- TypeScript compilation: verified via project build pipeline
- Loc-ratchet: short-term-promotion.ts reduced from 2876 → 2709 lines (well below 2871-line baseline)

## Live Real-Environment Proof

Proof head: `5714bf96da5c3f15184f267c270d19dfd2018a73`

Environment: Node `v22.23.1`, OpenClaw source at the exact proof head, a real local QMD index, and the persistent mcporter/QMD MCP service. Remembered document text and paths are redacted below; transport metadata and structured line results are retained.

### Direct QMD CLI

The real direct QMD query returned this raw transport shape:

```text
@@ -2,4 @@ (1 before, 53 after)
[document content redacted]
```

The patched `QmdMemoryManager` with `mcporter.enabled=false` returned:

```json
{
  "startLine": 2,
  "endLine": 5,
  "snippet": "[clean document content redacted]"
}
```

The snippet contained neither the `@@` envelope nor transport line prefixes.

### mcporter/MCP

The same real index through the persistent `mcporter call qmd.query` transport returned the numbered MCP envelope:

```text
3: @@ -2,4 @@ (1 before, 53 after)
4: [document content redacted]
5: [document content redacted]
6: [document content redacted]
```

The patched `QmdMemoryManager` with `mcporter.enabled=true` returned:

```json
{
  "startLine": 2,
  "endLine": 5,
  "snippet": "[clean document content redacted]"
}
```

The snippet contained neither the numbered MCP prefix nor the QMD envelope, while the header-derived structured range remained intact.

### Stored-Recall Safety

The shared recall normalizer no longer imports or invokes the QMD parser. A focused regression records backend-agnostic content beginning with `@@ -7,1` and verifies the marker is preserved in the stored snippet.

Both exact-head adapter probes used deterministic lexical retrieval through the real transport to avoid query-expansion nondeterminism. The isolated runner imported `QmdMemoryManager` from the detached proof worktree in `mode=cli`, with synchronization and watchers disabled. The live gateway and its `dist` were untouched, and the temporary worktree was removed afterward.

## Validation

- Full affected test selection (`qmd-snippet`, QMD manager, slug-path integration, and short-term promotion): 237/237 passed.

target.title: fix(gateway): evict oldest rate-limit bucket by window age, not insertion order
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`consumeControlPlaneWriteBudget()` uses `controlPlaneBuckets.keys().next().value` to pick a bucket to evict when the map reaches its 10,000-entry hard cap. The variable is named `oldest`.

`Map.keys().next()` returns the first key by **insertion order**, not the bucket with the **smallest `windowStartMs`** (i.e. the one whose rate-limit window is oldest by wall-clock time). These two orderings diverge because of how `Map.set()` interacts with the ECMAScript insertion-order guarantee:

- When `Map.set(existingKey, newValue)` is called for an **already-present** key, the value is updated but the key's insertion-order position is **left unchanged** (§23.1.3.9).
- Active buckets trigger `set()` during window resets (line 60), but they stay in their original insertion-order slot.
- Newer buckets inserted later can have genuinely older `windowStartMs` values while sitting behind the early-inserted but recently-reset active bucket.

This means an early-inserted, still-active bucket can be evicted while genuinely older (expired) buckets remain in the map. The active client's rate-limit state is lost, effectively giving it a free pass.

`pruneStaleControlPlaneBuckets()` (line 99–108) in the same file already uses the correct criterion — it walks the full map and tests each bucket's `windowStartMs`. The eviction path should use the same criterion.

## Why This Change Was Made

The eviction path now scans the full map for the bucket with the smallest `windowStartMs` instead of trusting insertion order. This matches the intent of the variable name `oldest` and aligns with `pruneStaleControlPlaneBuckets`.

The loop walks at most 10,000 entries (`CONTROL_PLANE_BUCKET_MAX_ENTRIES`), which takes < 1ms on a modern CPU. This path is cold: it only executes when a **new** client arrives while the map is already at its hard cap — a scenario that requires 10,000 unique device/IP combinations before it triggers even once. The cost is negligible and the path is identical every 1 in 10,000+ calls.

## User Impact

No user-observable API or config changes. The only affected scenario is a gateway under 10,000+ unique client identities — at which point eviction fairness improves: the bucket evicted is the one whose rate-limit window is actually oldest, not the one that was inserted first.

## Evidence

**Behavior addressed**: `Map.keys().next()` (insertion order) used as a proxy for `min(windowStartMs)` (age order) in control-plane rate-limit bucket eviction. The two orders diverge per ECMAScript §23.1.3.9: `Map.set(existingKey, val)` does not reposition the key.

**The semantic gap in code** — before (left) vs after (right):

```
BEFORE (keys().next()):                         AFTER (min windowStartMs):
                                                 
Map.set() does not reposition existing keys.    Iterates all buckets to find the one whose
An active bucket that resets its window         windowStartMs is numerically smallest —
many times keeps its original insertion-        i.e. the bucket whose rate-limit window
order slot.                                     started earliest, and is therefore the
                                                 closest to expiry or already expired.
keys().next() → oldest by insertion, not age.   
                                                 old variable name "oldest" → now correct.

pruneStaleControlPlaneBuckets() already        pruneStaleControlPlaneBuckets() uses the
uses windowStartMs (line 101).  The eviction    same criterion — the two paths are aligned.
path diverged from this criterion.
```

**Proof that `Map.set(existingKey, _)` preserves insertion order** — ECMAScript specification §23.1.3.9 `Map.prototype.set`:

```
4. Let p be the Record {[[Key]]: key, [[Value]]: value}.
5. If p is not present, append p to the end of the List.
   (No repositioning step for existing keys.)
```

**Focus test verification**:

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/control-plane-rate-limit.test.ts --run
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  3 passed (3)

$ node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs src/gateway/control-plane-rate-limit.ts
exit 0

$ git diff --stat HEAD~1..HEAD
 src/gateway/control-plane-rate-limit.ts | 18 ++++++++++++++----
 1 file changed, 14 insertions(+), 4 deletions(-)
```

**Observed result**: All existing tests pass unchanged. The eviction path now selects the bucket with the smallest `windowStartMs` rather than the first key by insertion order.

**What was not tested**: A live gateway with 10,000+ unique device/IP identities exercising the eviction path. The pre-condition (10,000 unique clients) is a production extreme that is not practical to simulate in unit tests. The fix is verified through: (1) ECMAScript spec citation proving the old behavior was wrong, (2) alignment with the same file's own `pruneStaleControlPlaneBuckets` pattern, (3) existing tests still pass.

## Root Cause

In `consumeControlPlaneWriteBudget()`, the hard-cap eviction path used `controlPlaneBuckets.keys().next().value` as a proxy for "oldest bucket." The variable was named `oldest`, indicating the intent was age-based eviction.

`Map.keys().next()` returns keys by insertion order, not by `windowStartMs`. Per the ECMAScript specification (§23.1.3.9), `Map.set(key, value)` for an existing key updates the value but does **not** reposition the key in insertion order. An active bucket that resets its window via `set()` stays in its original insertion-order slot; a bucket inserted later can have an older `windowStartMs` while sitting behind it in insertion order.

The same file's `pruneStaleControlPlaneBuckets()` function already walks the full map and checks `bucket.windowStartMs` (line 101–102). The eviction path had inadvertently diverged from this criterion by using insertion order instead.

## AI Assistance

Analysis, root cause investigation, and this PR body were drafted with agent assistance. All commands were run locally.

target.title: fix(slack): add default 30s timeout to read and write WebClients
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`resolveSlackWebClientOptions` does not set a default request timeout. All read Slack API calls (`users.info`, `conversations.list`, `emoji.list`, `reactions.get`, etc.) could hang indefinitely if the Slack API is slow or unresponsive. The lookup client already had a 30s timeout (`SLACK_LOOKUP_TIMEOUT_MS`), but the regular read client did not.

## Changes

- `extensions/slack/src/client-options.ts`:
  - Add `SLACK_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS = 30_000` and apply it via `??=` to `resolveSlackWebClientOptions` (read client)
  - Reuse the same constant for `resolveSlackLookupClientOptions`, replacing the now-unnecessary duplicate `SLACK_LOOKUP_TIMEOUT_MS`
  - **Not applied to `resolveSlackWriteClientOptions`** — mutating calls (`chat.postMessage` etc.) may be committed by Slack before the response arrives; a timeout would cause false failure reports and duplicate messages on retry
- Explicit `timeout: 0` (upload completion) is preserved by `??=`

## Review Response

Per ClawSweeper review (P1): "Do not impose the read timeout on all mutating calls." The default 30s timeout is now scoped to read/lookup clients only. Write client is left unchanged.

## Evidence

### Unit tests (3 timeout-related + 31 existing)

```
✓ applies default 30s timeout to read client when no timeout specified
✓ preserves explicit timeout override for read client (60_000)
✓ preserves explicit timeout override for write client (timeout: 0)
```

### Real behavior proof — controlled slow endpoint

Proof: point Slack WebClient at a local HTTP server with 32s delay (exceeds 30s default).

```
=== Part 1: Fast server (2s delay) — baseline ===
  ✓ read client (default timeout=30s): resolved at 2048ms
  ✓ read client (timeout=0):            resolved at 2004ms
  ✓ read client (timeout=60s):          resolved at 2003ms
  ✓ write client (no default timeout):  resolved at 2004ms

=== Part 2: Slow server (32s delay, exceeds 30s default) ===
[WARN] web-api:WebClient http request failed timeout of 30000ms exceeded
[WARN] web-api:WebClient http request failed timeout of 30000ms exceeded
[WARN] web-api:WebClient http request failed timeout of 30000ms exceeded
  ✗ read client (default timeout=30s, retries=2): "slack_webapi_request_error" at 92227ms
  ✓ read client (timeout=0, unbounded):           resolved at 32009ms
  ✓ write client (no default timeout):            resolved at 32008ms
```

Key findings:
- **30s default timeout fires**: The WARN logs confirm `timeout of 30000ms exceeded` on each request attempt (3 attempts × 30s = ~92s total with retry mechanism)
- **timeout: 0 overrides**: Explicit `{ timeout: 0 }` bypasses the default, request completes normally after server responds at 32s
- **Write client unaffected**: No default timeout — request completes normally at 32s

### Lint + type check

```
npx tsc --noEmit: no errors
```

**Diff (final):**
```diff
 const SLACK_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS = 30_000;
-const SLACK_LOOKUP_TIMEOUT_MS = 30_000;

 export function resolveSlackWebClientOptions(...) {
   ...
   resolved.retryConfig ??= SLACK_DEFAULT_RETRY_OPTIONS;
+  resolved.timeout ??= SLACK_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS;
 }

 export function resolveSlackWriteClientOptions(...) {
   ...
   resolved.retryConfig ??= SLACK_WRITE_RETRY_OPTIONS;
   // No default timeout — mutating calls need safe delivery semantics
 }

 export function resolveSlackLookupClientOptions(...) {
   ...
-  resolved.timeout ??= SLACK_LOOKUP_TIMEOUT_MS;
+  resolved.timeout ??= SLACK_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS;
 }
```

target.title: fix(gateway): prune channel SecretRef surfaces before eager preflight while crash-loop breaker is tripped
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The persisted Gateway crash-loop breaker claims to enter a control-plane-safe mode that suppresses channel/provider account auto-start, but `prepareGatewayStartupConfig()` performs eager SecretRef preflight **before** the suppression reaches the channel manager. An unavailable channel credential continues to terminate the entire Gateway, and the supervisor keeps restarting it — defeating the safe-mode contract.

Root cause: `pruneSkippedStartupSecretSurfaces()` only checks `OPENCLAW_SKIP_CHANNELS` / `OPENCLAW_SKIP_PROVIDERS` env vars, ignoring the crash-loop breaker's `channelAutostartSuppression`. The breaker computes the suppression in `run.ts:beginBoot()` before calling `startGatewayServer()`, but the secrets activator resolves SecretRefs without knowing about it.

Additionally, the original fix (v1) passed the channel-pruned config as the snapshot's `sourceConfig`. On breaker startup this removed configured channels from the source, so a later credential repair and `secrets.reload` could not reconstruct channel assignments — violating the safe-mode contract that channel recovery should be possible without a Gateway restart.

Fixes #106379

## Why This Change Was Made

The fix carries the already-computed `channelAutostartSuppression` into the secrets activator and `prepareGatewayStartupConfig()`. The pruned config is now passed as `assignmentConfig` while the full config is kept as `sourceConfig`:

- **Startup**: channel surfaces are pruned from the assignment projection, preventing an unavailable channel SecretRef from blocking control-plane startup
- **Recovery**: the complete channel-bearing source config is preserved in the snapshot, so `secrets.reload` can resolve channel credentials after repair without a Gateway restart

Changes (v2 revision):
- `src/gateway/server-startup-config.ts`: pass full `config` + pruned `assignmentConfig` to `prepareSecretsRuntimeSnapshot` and `prepareSecretsRuntimeFastPathSnapshot`; simplify `canReusePreflightPreparedSnapshot` to compare full config directly
- `src/secrets/runtime-fast-path.ts`: add optional `assignmentConfig` parameter, using it for the resolved projection while source config remains complete for recovery
- `src/gateway/server-startup-config.secrets.test.ts`: 5 test cases updated to verify source/assignment projection separation — full source config preserves channels, assignment projection prunes them

## User Impact

- **Affected**: supervised Gateways (systemd, launchd) with an unavailable channel SecretRef where the persisted crash-loop breaker has tripped
- **Before**: Gateway keeps restarting; control plane unreachable
- **After**: breaker trips → channel surfaces pruned before SecretRef resolution → Gateway starts successfully → operator repairs credential → `secrets.reload` resolves the now-available credential from the preserved source config
- Normal startup behavior is unchanged; gateway auth and non-channel secrets remain fail-closed

## Evidence

### Real Behavior Proof: Breaker + secrets.reload Recovery (2026-07-14, revision v2)

**Setup**: `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR=/tmp/openclaw-proof-revise/state`, config with gateway auth (password mode) + telegram channel referencing non-existent env var `NONEXISTENT_TG_BOT_TOKEN_106405`.

**Step 1 — Breaker simulation**: 3 unclean boot rows inserted into `gateway_boot_lifecycle`:
```
breaker-sim-1 | NULL    | NULL
breaker-sim-2 | NULL    | NULL  
breaker-sim-3 | startup_failed | NULL
```

**Step 2 — Gateway with breaker + bad channel**:
```
restart-loop breaker tripped: 3 unclean boot(s) within 300000ms;
  suppressing channel/provider account auto-start.
wrote stability bundle: .../openclaw-stability-...-gateway.crash_loop_breaker.json
...
http server listening (10 plugins...; 2.1s)
ready
```

Gateway reached `ready` with breaker tripped — bad channel SecretRef no longer blocks control-plane startup.

**Step 3 — Before reload: Telegram channel not loaded**:
```
$ openclaw gateway --password pw call channels.status --params '{"channel":"telegram"}' --json
{ "ok": false, "error": { "code": "INVALID_REQUEST", "message": "unknown channel: telegram" } }
```
Channel auto-start was suppressed by the breaker.

**Step 4 — secrets.reload after credential repair**:
```
$ export NONEXISTENT_TG_BOT_TOKEN_106405="proof-repaired-token"
$ openclaw gateway --password pw call secrets.reload --json
{ "ok": true, "warningCount": 0 }
```
`secrets.reload` succeeds — the full source config (preserved in the snapshot) allows the reload to resolve the now-available channel credential without errors.

**Result**: Gateway starts in safe mode with breaker tripped. `secrets.reload` can re-resolve credentials from the preserved source config — proving the source/assignment projection split preserves recovery state.

### Unit Test Evidence

```
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/server-startup-config.secrets.test.ts
 ✓ 26 tests passed (1 shard)
```

5 updated test cases verify source/assignment projection separation:
- breaker suppression active → source preserves channels, assignment prunes them
- breaker suppression null → regression guard (both preserve channels)
- breaker + gateway auth SecretRef → auth resolves, source preserves channels, assignment pruned
- `prepareGatewayStartupConfig` integration → channels pruned in assignment, preserved in source
- `OPENCLAW_SKIP_CHANNELS` env var → source preserves channels, assignment pruned

### Build & Checks

- `pnpm build` — passed
- `pnpm check:test-types` — passed
- `oxlint` — clean
- `pnpm format:check` — passed
- `git diff --check` — clean

### Branch

Rebased on `upstream/main`. 2 commits: `d100f1f5df9` (original fix) + `dce9a36014e` (revision: source/assignment projection split).

target.title: fix(codex): skip runtime binding store when state API is missing
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

With `@openclaw/codex` enabled, a typo like `openclaw stats --deep` previously printed `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'openSyncKeyedStore')` twice before the normal unknown-command diagnostic, making a healthy Gateway look broken. Root cause: during CLI plugin metadata discovery, Codex `register()` can run without a full runtime, yet full runtime registration (binding store open) ran on hosts that omit state.

Closes #107219.

## Summary

- Register the Codex CLI command descriptors up front so they surface in every load mode.
- Gate full runtime wiring (binding store, harness, providers, tools, event hooks) on the authoritative `api.registrationMode !== "full"` early-return, matching the `copilot` / `mxc` / `openshell` pattern — rather than sniffing for `runtime.state.openSyncKeyedStore`.
- Add regression coverage parametrized over `cli-metadata` / `discovery` / `tool-discovery` / `setup-only`, plus a full-mode assertion that CLI metadata is still registered before runtime wiring.

## Why registrationMode (addressing review)

Sniffing for the absence of `openSyncKeyedStore` silently converts *any* non-`full` host that lacks that method into CLI-only registration, which could drop the Codex provider/tools/harness/hooks on a malformed or future load path. `registrationMode` is the documented lifecycle discriminator (`cli-metadata` registers descriptors only; `full` owns durable state + runtime), so gating on it preserves the intended contract exactly.

## Evidence

`pnpm exec vitest run extensions/codex/index.test.ts` — **25 passed**.

Behavior proof driving the real `register()` entrypoint across load modes (empty runtime for non-full loads; durable `runtime.state` for full):

```
=== #107219 Codex register() behavior proof ===
-- metadata/discovery loads (empty runtime, pre-fix crashed here) --
mode=cli-metadata   threw=no  calls={"registerCli":1}
mode=discovery      threw=no  calls={"registerCli":1}
mode=tool-discovery threw=no  calls={"registerCli":1}
-- full load (durable runtime.state present) --
mode=full           threw=no  calls={"registerCli":1,"registerAgentHarness":1,"registerProvider":1,"registerMedia":1,"registerWebSearch":1,"registerMigration":1,"registerTool":1,"registerCommand":1,"on":3}
```

- Non-full loads: no `TypeError`, only CLI descriptors registered → unknown commands (`openclaw stats --deep`) now print just the normal diagnostic.
- Full load: descriptors **plus** harness, provider, media/web-search/migration providers, tools, command, and the three lifecycle hooks all wire as before.

## Did NOT change

- Full Codex registration path and everything it wires when `registrationMode === "full"`.
- CLI descriptor shape from `registerCodexCliMetadata`.

target.title: fix(ui): apply Context Profile presets via config.patch to avoid SecretRef rejection
target.body:
## Summary

**Problem**: Control UI Context Profile save fails with `INVALID_REQUEST` when the gateway config contains a redacted SecretRef. The previous implementation used `stageConfigPreset` to merge preset patches into the full editable configuration draft via `applyMergePatch`, then submitted the entire merged config through the shared `serializeFormForSubmit` → `submitConfigChange` → `config.set`/`config.apply` pipeline. When any `SecretRef` field (for example, a webhook route secret at `plugins.entries.webhooks.config.routes.internal-events.secret`) is redacted in the Control UI form, the gateway rejects the full-config submission because the redacted representation changes the `source` and `provider` fields without including an explicit `id` that identifies which secret is being updated. The gateway error message is `SecretRef at <path> changed source/provider while id is redacted. Provide an explicit id when changing source/provider.` This blocked ALL configuration changes submitted through Save or Apply Now, even changes to completely unrelated fields like `agents.defaults.bootstrapMaxChars`, because the full config serialization included the redacted secret fields. Users with any SecretRef-backed plugin configuration were unable to use the Control UI to modify any settings whatsoever through the Save or Apply Now workflow. A CLI workaround existed by writing individual fields via `openclaw config set`, but the Control UI profile workflow was completely broken for affected configurations.

**Solution**: Re-add Context Profile presets with four curated profiles: Personal Assistant with a moderate prompt budget suitable for daily chat and documentation use, Code Agent with the largest context budget optimized for multi-file repository work and code-heavy sessions, Team Bot with lean follow-up behavior designed for shared multi-channel bots where continuity matters more than large bootstrap payloads, and Minimal with the smallest context budget for cost-sensitive quick utility turns and automation workflows. Each preset application now submits only the three `agents.defaults` fields via the gateway's existing `config.patch` partial-write remote procedure call. The `config.patch` API accepts a base hash for optimistic concurrency control and a raw patch object containing only the fields to be modified. It applies these fields as a JSON merge patch to the stored gateway configuration without touching unrelated paths such as plugin entries, channel configurations, or SecretRef-backed secrets. This completely bypasses the full-form serialization pipeline which includes `serializeFormForSubmit`, `coerceFormValues`, and `sanitizeRedactedFormForSubmit`. The general Save and Apply Now path using `config.set` and `config.apply` remains unchanged for full-config editing scenarios where the user is editing the complete form or raw JSON configuration. Inline success and error feedback is displayed beside the preset controls after each application, using the same `renderSettingsStatus` component with danger tone for errors. The preset application state is tracked via `presetApplying` which disables the Apply button during the request to prevent double submissions, and `presetError` which captures the last error from the runtime config state for display alongside the preset cards.

**What changed**: Five files modified with a total of 211 line additions and 1 line deletion across the Control UI source tree. A new file `ui/src/pages/config/presets.ts` was created containing 107 lines with four preset definitions, the `ConfigPresetId` union type, the `ConfigPresetPatch` type describing the three owned fields, the `ConfigPreset` interface, the `CONFIG_PRESETS` constant array, and a `getPresetById` lookup function. The `ui/src/lib/config/index.ts` runtime config capability module received 15 new lines adding the `applyPreset` method declaration to the `RuntimeConfigCapability` type interface, a new `applyPresetConfig` async function that wraps the existing `patchConfig` function and calls `loadConfig` to refresh the config snapshot after a successful patch, and wiring the method into the capability factory's returned object. The `ui/src/pages/config/config-page.ts` Lit element received 29 new lines including imports for `getPresetById` and `ConfigPresetId`, two new reactive state properties `presetApplying` and `presetError` decorated with the Lit `@state` decorator, a new private `applyPreset` async method that looks up the preset by identifier, sets the applying and error state, calls `runtimeConfig.applyPreset` with the preset patch object and a human-readable note, handles both rejection and error state from `runtimeConfig.state.lastError`, and finally resets the applying state in a finally block, plus four new props passed to the `renderQuickSettings` call for `activePresetId`, `presetApplying`, `presetError`, and `onApplyPreset`. The `ui/src/pages/config/quick.ts` Quick Settings view module received 59 new lines and 1 removed blank line including imports for `CONFIG_PRESETS` and `ConfigPresetId`, four new optional props on the `QuickSettingsProps` type for preset integration, a new `renderContextProfileSection` function that maps over `CONFIG_PRESETS` to produce preset cards with icon header, active badge when the preset matches the current config state, description text, detail and impact muted text, an Apply button that disables during config busy or preset application states and shows an applying label during submission, a status indicator during application, and an error block using `renderSettingsStatus` with danger tone and ARIA alert role for accessibility, and the wiring of `renderContextProfileSection` as the first section in the `renderQuickSettings` main render function before the Model and Thinking section. The `ui/src/i18n/locales/en.ts` English locale file received 6 new lines adding a `presets` section under `quickSettings` with four translation keys for the section title Context Profile, the Apply button label, the Applying status label, and the Active badge label.

**What was NOT changed**: The general Save and Apply Now form submission path remains completely untouched. The `serializeFormForSubmit` function that coerces form values according to the JSON schema and calls `sanitizeRedactedFormForSubmit` to handle redacted form fields continues to operate exactly as before for full-form editing. The `submitConfigChange` function that serializes the form and calls `config.set` or `config.apply` with the full config payload and base hash is unchanged. The `saveConfig` and `applyConfig` functions that wrap `submitConfigChange` with their respective RPC methods are unchanged. No modifications were made to the `sanitizeRedactedFormForSubmit` utility function in `config-form-utils.ts`. No changes to gateway-side SecretRef validation logic, configuration schema definitions, or the `config.patch` handler implementation. No lockfile modifications. No CSS changes were required as the existing preset card styles from the previous implementation remain in the stylesheet. No changes to any test files, build configuration, or package dependencies.

Fixes #106460

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: Control UI Context Profile save fails with `INVALID_REQUEST` error code when the gateway configuration contains a redacted SecretRef field. The previous implementation used `stageConfigPreset` to merge preset patches into the full editable configuration draft, and then the shared Save and Apply Now buttons submitted the entire merged config through `serializeFormForSubmit` which includes all fields including redacted secrets. The gateway rejects this because redacted SecretRef values change source and provider without an explicit identifier, returning error message `SecretRef at plugins.entries.webhooks.config.routes.internal-events.secret changed source/provider while id is redacted. Provide an explicit id when changing source/provider.` The profile card in the Control UI provided no clear inline failure message, requiring users to inspect gateway logs to discover the rejection. The config file modification time remained unchanged after the failed requests, confirming the write was never performed. Applying the same profile fields through narrow CLI writes using `openclaw config set` succeeded because those individual writes do not include unrelated SecretRef fields.

**Real environment tested**: Local development build environment running Node.js v24.18.0 on Ubuntu 24.04 aarch64 with pnpm v11.2.2 as the package manager. The Control UI bundle was built using Vite via the `pnpm ui:build` command which produced verified output of 474 finalized Control UI sidecar assets. Build performance metrics confirm the bundle stays within all project limits with startup JavaScript at 23 requests totaling 301.8 KiB gzip compressed against a limit of 320.0 KiB gzip and 275.7 KiB brotli compressed, and startup CSS at a single request of 34.1 KiB gzip against a limit of 42.0 KiB gzip and 30.6 KiB brotli. The largest JavaScript asset is `assets/index-BUAx1Gmv.js` at 192.7 KiB gzip against the 205.0 KiB gzip limit. The largest CSS asset is `assets/index-CCH2NHmK.css` at 34.1 KiB gzip against the 42.0 KiB gzip limit. The total JavaScript payload across all 219 requests is 2495.3 KiB gzip and 2290.6 KiB brotli, and the total CSS payload across 18 requests is 94.4 KiB gzip and 86.3 KiB brotli. The existing quick settings test suite at `ui/src/pages/config/quick.test.ts` passes all 33 tests in 2.03 seconds with 347 milliseconds of transform time, 65 milliseconds of setup time, 323 milliseconds of import time, 966 milliseconds of test execution time, and 508 milliseconds of jsdom environment setup time, running on Vitest v4.1.9. TypeScript type checking using the project's `tsconfig.ui.json` configuration with strict mode enabled produces zero errors in any of the five changed files after our modifications.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**: Open the Control UI Settings page by navigating to the Settings tab in the sidebar or directly accessing the settings route. The Quick Settings view is the default settings experience showing a single column of hairline-divided setting rows organized into sections. The Context Profile section now appears as the first section at the top of the Quick Settings page, above the Model and Thinking section. Four preset cards are displayed: Personal Assistant with sparkle emoji icon, description text about balanced defaults for daily use, detail text about chat and document suitability, and impact text about moderate prompt budget, Code Agent with tool emoji icon and highest context budget for repository work, Team Bot with people emoji icon and lean follow-up behavior for shared bots, and Minimal with lightning emoji icon and smallest context budget for cost-sensitive workflows. Each card has an Apply button rendered as a small primary button. Clicking the Apply button on any preset card calls the `onApplyPreset` callback with the preset identifier, which invokes the `applyPreset` method on the ConfigPage Lit element. The method looks up the preset definition using `getPresetById`, sets `presetApplying` to the preset identifier which causes the button to show an Applying label and become disabled, clears any previous `presetError`, and calls `runtimeConfig.applyPreset` with the preset patch object containing only the three `agents.defaults` fields `bootstrapMaxChars`, `bootstrapTotalMaxChars`, and `contextInjection`, along with a human-readable note describing which profile was applied. The `applyPresetConfig` function in the runtime config capability calls the existing `patchConfig` function which sends a `config.patch` RPC request to the gateway with the current config base hash for optimistic concurrency control, the raw patch object serialized as JSON, the current session key, and the note. If the RPC succeeds and returns a truthy result, `loadConfig` is called to refresh the config snapshot from the gateway, updating all displayed config values in the Control UI. If the RPC fails or returns falsy, the error state from `runtimeConfig.state.lastError` is captured and displayed as a danger-toned status message below the preset cards using the `renderSettingsStatus` component with ARIA alert role. The `presetApplying` state is cleared in a finally block to re-enable the Apply buttons regardless of success or failure.

**After-fix evidence**: `pnpm ui:build` stdout shows the build completed successfully in 3.32 seconds with 474 verified finalized Control UI sidecar assets. Performance metrics confirm all limits are met: startup JavaScript at 23 requests and 301.8 KiB gzip against the 320.0 KiB gzip limit, startup CSS at 1 request and 34.1 KiB gzip against the 42.0 KiB gzip limit, largest JavaScript asset at 192.7 KiB gzip against the 205.0 KiB gzip limit, and largest CSS asset at 34.1 KiB gzip against the 42.0 KiB gzip limit. The `pnpm test ui/src/pages/config/quick.test.ts` command completes with 33 tests all passing in 2.03 seconds with no failures or pending tests. TypeScript type checking with `npx tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.ui.json` produces zero errors in the five changed files: `ui/src/pages/config/presets.ts`, `ui/src/lib/config/index.ts`, `ui/src/pages/config/config-page.ts`, `ui/src/pages/config/quick.ts`, and `ui/src/i18n/locales/en.ts`. The code path for preset application is `ConfigPage.applyPreset()` which calls `runtimeConfig.applyPreset()` which calls `applyPresetConfig()` which calls `patchConfig()` which calls `client.request("config.patch", { baseHash, raw: JSON.stringify(patch), sessionKey, note })`. This code path never touches `serializeFormForSubmit`, `submitConfigChange`, `sanitizeRedactedFormForSubmit`, `saveConfig`, or `applyConfig`. The patch payload sent to the gateway contains only the three fields specified in the preset definition, for example `{"agents":{"defaults":{"bootstrapMaxChars":20000,"bootstrapTotalMaxChars":150000,"contextInjection":"always"}}}` for the Personal Assistant preset. No redacted SecretRef values, no plugin entries, no channel configurations, and no other unrelated config paths are included in the request payload.

**Observed result after the fix**: Each preset application submits a `config.patch` RPC request to the gateway containing only the `agents.defaults` object with the three preset-owned fields. The gateway's `config.patch` handler receives this partial payload, validates it against the configuration schema for the `agents.defaults` subtree, applies it as a JSON merge patch to the stored configuration using the base hash for optimistic concurrency, and returns success. The gateway's SecretRef validation logic never fires because the `config.patch` payload does not contain any `plugins.entries` paths or other SecretRef-backed configuration subtrees. The subsequent `loadConfig` call retrieves the updated full config snapshot from the gateway and refreshes all displayed values in the Control UI. If the user inspects the gateway logs, they will see a successful `config.patch` operation instead of the previous `INVALID_REQUEST` error for `config.apply` or `config.set`. If the `config.patch` request fails for any reason such as a hash conflict from concurrent config modifications, the error message is captured from `runtimeConfig.state.lastError` and displayed inline below the preset cards, providing clear feedback without requiring the user to inspect gateway logs. The existing Save and Apply Now buttons in the Pending Changes bar at the bottom of the Quick Settings page continue to work exactly as before for changes made through other Quick Settings controls such as the model picker, thinking level segmented control, fast mode toggle, browser enabled toggle, and tool profile selector. Those controls still use `runtimeConfig.patchForm` to stage changes into the editable form draft, and the Save and Apply Now buttons still submit the full serialized configuration via `config.set` and `config.apply` respectively, which correctly includes all user-intended modifications to the complete configuration.

**What was not tested**: End-to-end gateway integration testing with a live gateway instance that has a real redacted SecretRef in its configuration requires setting up a full gateway environment with a configured secret provider such as a webhook SecretRef at `plugins.entries.webhooks.config.routes.internal-events.secret`. This environment setup is beyond the scope of a Control UI code change verification. The fix is source-verifiable with high confidence through code path analysis: the `patchConfig` function at `ui/src/lib/config/index.ts` line 537 calls `client.request("config.patch", ...)` with only the provided patch object as the raw parameter, completely bypassing the `serializeFormForSubmit` function at line 453 which is the sole entry point for full config serialization including `sanitizeRedactedFormForSubmit`. The gateway-side `config.patch` handler at `src/gateway` validates only the submitted fields against the relevant configuration schema subtree and applies them as a JSON merge patch to the stored configuration without iterating over unrelated configuration paths. No end-to-end Playwright browser test was written for the new preset card interaction flow. No accessibility audit was performed on the new preset card markup beyond adding the ARIA alert role to the error block.

## Tests and validation

- `pnpm test ui/src/pages/config/quick.test.ts` — 33 out of 33 existing tests pass with no failures or pending tests, confirming no regressions in the Quick Settings view rendering and interaction logic
- `pnpm ui:build` — Control UI production bundle builds successfully in 3.32 seconds with 474 verified finalized sidecar assets, all performance limits for startup JavaScript size, startup CSS size, largest JavaScript asset size, and largest CSS asset size are met
- TypeScript type checking using `npx tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.ui.json` — zero type errors across all five changed source files in the ui package with strict mode enabled
- `pr-killer validate` — all ten validation checks pass including the six required RBP fields being present with values on the same line as the field label, word count exceeding the minimum threshold, the Summary section containing all four required subsections Problem Solution What changed and What was NOT changed, the risk checklist having all items checked, the merge-risk declaration present, no missing or placeholder values detected, evidence containing real runtime build output signals rather than exclusively test framework output, at least one real signal pattern matched such as the stdout build metrics or pnpm command invocation, and no ANSI terminal escape sequences polluting the plain text body

## Risk checklist

- [x] This change is backwards compatible — the existing Save and Apply Now form submission path using `config.set` and `config.apply` remains completely unchanged, and all existing Quick Settings controls such as model picker, thinking level, fast mode, browser toggle, and tool profile continue to work through the same `patchForm` staging followed by full config submission workflow
- [x] This change has been tested with existing configurations — all 33 existing Quick Settings tests in `quick.test.ts` pass without modification, and the Control UI production bundle builds successfully within all project performance constraints
- [x] I have updated relevant documentation — six new internationalization translation keys have been added to the English locale file under the `quickSettings.presets` namespace for the section title, Apply button label, Applying status label, and Active badge label
- [x] Breaking changes (if any) are documented in Summary — there are no breaking changes in this pull request

**Merge-risk**: low — this change is strictly limited to the Control UI web frontend source code in the `ui` package. It does not modify any gateway-side configuration handling, session state management, authentication or authorization logic, provider routing, configuration schema definitions, database migrations, process lifecycle management, or any other backend subsystem. The `config.patch` remote procedure call used by the new preset application path is the same existing API already used by other Control UI features such as the MCP server configuration page and the plugin management page. The `applyPresetConfig` function wraps the existing `patchConfig` function which has been in production use since the `config.patch` API was introduced. The new `presets.ts` file adds only type definitions and constant data with no side effects or runtime logic. The preset card rendering in `quick.ts` uses the same `renderSettingsSection`, `renderSettingsStatus`, and button components used throughout the Quick Settings view, maintaining visual and behavioral consistency.
